title: Dynamic Allocation: new, delete and malloc
objectives: Explain the two-step mechanics of new (allocation then construction) and delete (destruction then release)
Compare malloc/free with new/delete across construction, type safety and failure behaviour
Apply the matching rules (new/delete, new[]/delete[], malloc/free) and explain why mixing them is undefined behaviour
Handle allocation failure correctly using std::bad_alloc and std::nothrow
motivation: Order books, ring buffers and price caches are all sized at runtime, so real systems allocate on the heap constantly. C++ hands you two allocation families - the C legacy malloc/free and the C++ new/delete expressions - and every ownership bug in the next lessons traces back to a misunderstanding of exactly one of them. Getting allocation mechanics, matching rules and failure modes right is the price of admission for everything that follows.

blocks.md: **malloc** comes from C: you ask for a number of raw bytes, it returns a void* to uninitialised memory (or a null pointer on failure), and nothing else happens - no constructor runs, no type is recorded. **new** is a C++ expression that does two things: it allocates enough bytes for the type (with correct alignment) and then *runs the constructor*, returning a properly typed T*. Correspondingly **free** just releases bytes, while **delete** runs the destructor first and then releases. A useful mental model: new = operator new (a malloc-like raw allocator) + constructor; delete = destructor + operator delete.

blocks.text: What new actually does - and what delete undoes

blocks.md: Because new constructs and delete destroys, they are the only correct partners for class types. For arrays, new[] must also *remember how many elements it created* (implementations store an element count, informally the *cookie*, just before the array), so that delete[] can run a destructor for every element before releasing the block. Destroying the right number of elements is not a formality: forgetting N std::string destructors leaks every buffer those strings own.

blocks.caption: new[]/delete[] track the element count so every destructor runs exactly once.

blocks.md: Plain new does not return null on failure - it **throws std::bad_alloc**. Writing `if (p == nullptr)` after a plain new is dead code. If you want the C-style contract, ask for it explicitly with `new (std::nothrow)`, which returns a null pointer on failure and lets you check. malloc keeps its C behaviour: NULL plus errno. One further subtlety: requesting zero bytes with new is legal and returns a unique, valid, non-null pointer that must still be deleted.

blocks.caption: std::nothrow gives new the C-style failure contract, for code that prefers checking to catching.

blocks.title: Mixing families is undefined behaviour
blocks.md: free()ing a pointer you got from new skips the destructor and confuses two different allocators; delete-ing malloc'd memory corrupts the heap. The matching rules are absolute: new↔delete, new[]↔delete[], malloc↔free. Using plain delete on a new[] array is a classic silent corruption: the cookie is ignored, only one element is destroyed, and the rest of the heap degrades unpredictably.

blocks.text: When to reach for the heap - and when not to

blocks.md: Dynamic allocation is the right tool when the size is known only at runtime, when the object must outlive the scope that creates it, or when the data is too big for the stack. But the default answer in modern C++ is neither new nor malloc - it is a container or smart pointer that calls new for you. `std::vector<Fill>` gives you runtime sizing with automatic cleanup; `std::unique_ptr<Fill>` (next lessons) gives you single-owner heap objects with zero manual deletes. Raw new/delete in application code is a code smell, kept only for library internals and interfacing with C.

blocks.title: The C boundary
blocks.md: You will meet malloc in C libraries and in allocators for POD buffers. The clean rule at the boundary: a block obtained from malloc is freed with free and never assumed to hold constructed objects; if a C API hands you memory that you must fill with real C++ objects, that is placement-new territory and belongs behind a well-tested wrapper.

blocks.caption: new[] hides an element-count cookie in front of the array; delete[] reads it to know how many destructors to run.

hints: Trace every path out of the function and ask 'who deletes buf?' on each.
An exception skips every statement between the allocation and the end of the function.
If the answer to (c) is no, the resource must be bound to something whose destructor runs during unwinding.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) The caller owns it: the function transfers ownership on return, which must be documented (or better, expressed in the type - return `std::unique_ptr<double[]>`). (b) The exception propagates out of process() and `buf` is simply lost: the heap block is unreachable but never freed - a **leak on every feed error**, and in a storm of feed errors the process dies of memory exhaustion. (c) Not robustly: you could wrap the call in try/catch, delete buf, and rethrow - but every future edit of the function must preserve that pattern; one early return added later re-opens the leak. (d) Return `std::vector<double>(n)` or `std::unique_ptr<double[]> buf = std::make_unique<double[]>(n)`: the destructor runs during stack unwinding, so no path can leak. This is RAII, formalised two lessons ahead.

independentExercise.prompt: An instrument cache holds up to N = 500,000 PriceLevel structs, where `struct PriceLevel { double px; long qty; };` (double: 8 bytes, long: 8 bytes). (a) How many bytes does `new PriceLevel[N]` request for the elements? (b) How many bytes does the equivalent malloc call request? (c) Which expression releases the new[] allocation correctly? (d) State precisely what goes wrong if plain `delete` (no brackets) is used instead. (e) On failure, what does `new PriceLevel[N]` do versus `new (std::nothrow) PriceLevel[N]`?
hints: (b) malloc takes the byte count you compute yourself.
(e) plain new throws a specific exception type on failure.
independentExercise.solution: (a) 500,000 × 16 = **8,000,000 bytes** (about 7.63 MiB). (b) The same 8,000,000 bytes - malloc is given `500000 * sizeof(PriceLevel)`; the difference is not size but that no constructors run and you get a void*. (c) `delete[] levels;` - the array form must match the array form. (d) Undefined behaviour: without the brackets only the *first* element (or none, for POD) is considered destroyed, the cookie is ignored, and the heap state becomes corrupted - typically crashing later, somewhere unrelated. (e) Plain new throws **std::bad_alloc** on failure; the nothrow form returns nullptr, which is the only version where a null check is meaningful.

commonMistakes: Checking for nullptr after a plain new: plain new throws std::bad_alloc instead of returning null; the check is dead code.
Pairing new[] with delete (no brackets), or free() with new - mismatched release is undefined behaviour.
Believing delete is 'the same as free plus nothing': delete runs the destructor first, which is the entire point for class types.
Computing malloc sizes by hand and forgetting alignment - new aligns automatically, malloc requires you to request aligned sizes yourself.
Requesting zero elements and assuming the pointer is null: new T[0] is valid, non-null, and must still be delete[]'d.
realWorldApplication: Every runtime-sized structure in a trading system - message buffers, book levels, fill logs - is born from new or a container that calls it. Understanding allocation mechanics is required reading before touching a memory pool or a custom allocator.
quantFinanceApplication: A market-data gateway pre-allocates a 64 MB message buffer with new[] at start-up: one 64 MB bad_alloc consideration at boot, zero allocations on the hot path afterwards - allocation policy *is* latency policy.
summary: new = allocate + construct (returns T*, throws std::bad_alloc); delete = destruct + release; malloc/free handle raw bytes with a NULL failure contract.
Matching rules are absolute: new↔delete, new[]↔delete[], malloc↔free - mixing them is undefined behaviour.
new[] records the element count (the cookie) so delete[] runs every element's destructor exactly once.
std::nothrow (or try/catch around bad_alloc) is the correct way to handle allocation failure; checking a plain new against nullptr is dead code.
Prefer containers and smart pointers, which perform dynamic allocation internally with guaranteed cleanup; raw new/delete belongs in library internals.

quiz.prompt: What is the key difference between `T* p = new T(args);` and `T* p = (T*)malloc(sizeof(T));`?
options: Nothing, they are interchangeable for any T
new allocates and constructs (runs the constructor) and throws on failure; malloc returns raw uninitialised bytes and returns NULL on failure
malloc is faster and therefore always preferred in C++
new returns a void* while malloc returns a typed pointer
quiz.explanation: new pairs allocation with construction and reports failure by throwing std::bad_alloc; malloc hands back raw bytes (constructor must be run manually, which is placement-new territory) and signals failure with NULL.
new int{7} value-initialises to 7; after *p += 3 it is 10; after delete, setting p to nullptr makes the comparison true, so bool prints as 1.
new int[3]{} value-initialises every element to 0, so after a[1] = 5 the elements are 0, 5, 0 - printed as 050. The single object new int{9} is value-initialised to 9.

quiz.prompt: On a platform where sizeof(int) == 4, how many bytes does the element storage of `new int[100]` occupy (ignore any implementation cookie)?
quiz.explanation: 100 elements × 4 bytes = 400 bytes. Implementations may add a hidden cookie for the element count, but the elements themselves occupy 400 bytes.

quiz.prompt: An array was created with `auto* s = new std::string[10];`. Which release is correct, and what happens with the wrong one?
options: delete s; the wrong one merely leaks
delete[] s; plain delete is undefined behaviour - only one element is destroyed and the heap may corrupt
free(s); free is the universal release for heap blocks
Both delete and delete[] are fine for arrays of POD types only
quiz.explanation: new[] must pair with delete[]: the bracket form reads the element-count cookie and destroys all 10 strings. Plain delete destroys (at most) one and releases the block once - undefined behaviour with real consequences for non-trivial types.

quiz.prompt: Select every true statement about dynamic allocation.
options: Deleting a null pointer is safe and does nothing
Memory obtained from malloc must be released with delete
new[] records the element count so delete[] can destroy all elements
A plain new expression returns nullptr when the heap is exhausted
quiz.explanation: delete on null is a guaranteed no-op, and the new[] cookie is what makes delete[] destroy every element. malloc memory pairs with free, and plain new throws std::bad_alloc on exhaustion rather than returning null.

flashcards.front: What are the two steps of `new T(args)` and the two steps of `delete p`?
flashcards.back: new: allocate raw memory (operator new), then run T's constructor. delete: run the destructor, then release memory (operator delete).

flashcards.front: The matching rules for allocation families
flashcards.back: new ↔ delete, new[] ↔ delete[], malloc ↔ free. Any cross-pairing is undefined behaviour.

flashcards.front: What does `delete p;` do when p is nullptr?
flashcards.back: Nothing - a guaranteed safe no-op. That is why setting pointers to null after delete makes double deletes harmless.

flashcards.front: Failure behaviour: plain new vs new(std::nothrow) vs malloc
flashcards.back: plain new throws std::bad_alloc; new(std::nothrow) returns nullptr; malloc returns NULL (and sets errno).
